items.q: What does this print?  x = [i*i for i in range(4)]
items.explain: range(4) is 0..3; squares are 0, 1, 4, 9. Comprehensions are the idiom AI code uses everywhere.

items.q: The GIL means threads in CPython cannot…
choices: Execute Python bytecode on two cores at once
Use the threading module at all
items.explain: The GIL serializes bytecode execution: threads help I/O-bound work (one waits while another runs) but not CPU-bound parallelism.

items.q: def f(a, b=[]): b.append(a); return b  — calling f(1) then f(2) returns…
items.explain: The default list is created once at def time and shared across calls — the classic mutable-default trap.

items.q: Which is the right tool for CPU-bound parallelism in CPython?
items.explain: multiprocessing sidesteps the GIL with separate processes; threading does not parallelize CPU-bound Python.

items.q: A virtual environment primarily gives you…
choices: An isolated package set per project
items.explain: venvs isolate dependencies per project so one project's numpy never breaks another's — reproducibility 101.

items.q: The strongest check that AI-generated code is correct is…
items.explain: Running once proves little; tests encode the contract. Verification discipline is the whole skill.

items.q: In NumPy, a (3,1) array added to a (4,) array broadcasts to…
items.explain: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions: (3,1) with (4,) becomes (3,4).

items.q: pandas groupby().agg() is the right tool when you need…
items.explain: groupby splits rows into groups; agg collapses each group to summary values — vectorized, no loops.

items.q: The most common cause of an unrealistically good validation score is…
items.explain: Leakage — validation data influencing training (via preprocessing fit on all data, duplicate rows, future features) — inflates scores that collapse in production.

items.q: A truncated y-axis on a bar chart is…
items.explain: Truncating the axis visually magnifies small differences. Honest charts start bars at zero unless there is a stated reason.

items.q: Vectorized NumPy code beats Python loops mainly because…
choices: The loop runs in compiled C over contiguous memory
NumPy uses the GPU by default
items.explain: Vectorized ops execute in optimized C on contiguous buffers — often 10-100x faster than interpreted per-element loops.

items.q: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting is…
items.explain: Preprocessing statistics must come from the training split only; fit on all data leaks test information into training.

items.q: On a 99%-negative fraud dataset, a model predicting ‘always negative’ scores 99% accuracy. The right response is…
choices: Switch to precision/recall or PR-AUC; accuracy is meaningless here
Balance the dataset by deleting negatives
Accuracy is the only valid metric
items.explain: Accuracy on imbalanced data rewards the majority-class constant predictor. Precision/recall or PR curves reveal the fraud-catching ability.

items.q: k-fold cross-validation primarily guards against…
choices: A lucky or unlucky single split misleading you
items.explain: Averaging over k folds reduces split luck; every row is validated exactly once.

items.q: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set is…
choices: Leakage: the test set becomes a validation set and scores inflate
items.explain: Any decision made using test data — including hyperparameter choice — contaminates the final estimate. Tune on validation, report once on test.

items.q: PCA is best described as…
choices: A linear projection onto directions of maximum variance
items.explain: PCA finds orthogonal directions capturing the most variance; it compresses features but knows nothing about labels.

items.q: L2 regularization (ridge) helps overfitting by…
choices: Penalizing large weights, shrinking them toward zero
items.explain: The penalty term keeps weights small, constraining model complexity without discrete feature removal (that is L1's sparsity).

items.q: In Q-learning, the agent balances exploration and exploitation commonly via…
items.explain: Epsilon-greedy explores randomly with probability epsilon and exploits otherwise — the standard first answer to the tradeoff.

items.q: Backpropagation computes…
choices: Gradients of the loss with respect to every parameter, via the chain rule
items.explain: Backprop is the chain rule applied layer by layer, giving each parameter its gradient so optimizers can update it.

items.q: Dropout helps generalization by…
choices: Randomly zeroing activations during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit
items.explain: Dropout forces redundant representations; at inference the full network runs (scaled), which is the regularization effect.

items.q: Early stopping needs a ________ to decide when to stop.
items.explain: Stop when validation loss stops improving — the test set must stay untouched until final reporting, or the estimate is biased.

items.q: A convolution layer suits images because…
choices: It is faster than dense layers only
Weight sharing gives translation equivariance with far fewer parameters
items.explain: The same filter slides across the image: a feature detector works wherever the feature appears, with shared weights.

items.q: Vanishing gradients in deep networks mean…
choices: Gradients shrink toward zero in early layers, stalling their learning
items.explain: Repeated multiplication of small derivatives starves early layers of signal — the problem residuals, normalization, and careful init address.

items.q: Transfer learning on a small image dataset usually means…
choices: Reusing a pretrained backbone, training a new head (and optionally fine-tuning)
Using a smaller learning rate of zero
items.explain: Pretrained features transfer; a fresh classifier head plus optional gentle fine-tuning beats from-scratch on small data.

items.q: Self-attention lets a token…
choices: Weigh every other token's relevance when forming its representation
items.explain: Attention computes pairwise relevance across the whole sequence — the parallelism and long-range modeling that beat recurrence.

items.q: GPT-style models differ from BERT-style models fundamentally in…
choices: Training objective: next-token prediction vs masked-token prediction
items.explain: Autoregressive (predict the next token) vs masked LM (fill the blanks): the objective shapes the task family each serves.

items.q: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) primarily addresses…
choices: Grounding answers in retrieved documents to cut hallucination
items.explain: RAG feeds relevant retrieved passages into the prompt so the model answers from provided sources instead of inventing.

items.q: Raising the sampling temperature toward 2.0 makes output…
choices: More random and diverse, eventually incoherent
items.explain: Temperature flattens the token distribution: higher means more randomness and creativity, lower means more determinism.

items.q: A GAN's generator improves because…
choices: It sees the real data directly
The discriminator's feedback signal pushes it to fool the discriminator
items.explain: The adversarial game: the discriminator learns to spot fakes, its gradients teach the generator to make better ones.

items.q: Chain-of-thought prompting can leak…
choices: Intermediate reasoning that may expose sensitive content or flawed logic the final answer hides
items.explain: Exposed reasoning traces can reveal private context or unsound steps — a real consideration in production agent design.
